selected_news.title: Anthropic allocates 5% of shares to public‑good fund
selected_news.summary: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listing Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing. The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. selected_news.source_headline: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
selected_news.article_text: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listing Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline The fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours “AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost It said that while it had already committed $200m to addressing the issue, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The fund will have the versatility to pursue them.” The company, which is preparing to list on the stock market, has called for a slowdown in breakneck development of AI, a warning later echoed by rivals such as OpenAI Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round. The company is reportedly considering a $1.5tn valuation when it floats on the stock market, with an IPO planned for November Last week, Anthropic said some of its AI models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners It said that once this happens, the models would be able to power themselves without the need of datacentres Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and founder of SpaceX, responded to Anthropic’s plans for a public benefit fund on social media by pledging to give some of his own shares away “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” he wrote. “This is what I will be doing.” He later announced: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.” Shares in SpaceX, which is listed on the Nasdaq in the US, rose by 1% in pre-market trading on Monday. The company has lost about 9% of its value since it joined the stock market in June OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, also reportedly engaged in early talks to give a 5% stake in its organisation to the US government Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, was established as a public benefit corporation. It means that all of the company’s directors must balance financial returns with its public interest mission

selected_news.source_headline: Foamy war? St Andrews students play out modern take on ancient ritual
selected_news.article_text: Scottish university’s annual tradition once involved giving out raisins but fancy dress and shaving cream now in vogue Nobody at the University of St Andrews in Scotland seems to remember how Raisin Monday became a giant foam fight. For 600 years, first-year students have taken part in the ritual of thanking older students for mentoring them through their first few weeks of university life Traditionally, freshers would give their elders a pound of raisins – hence the name. This Monday however, hundreds wore fancy dress as they streamed on to St Salvator’s lower college lawn at 11am armed with cans of shaving foam, covering one another in soapy clouds as they have for the past few decades. Groups of students dress as Smurfs, mice, bananas, grandmas, sunflowers and chefs to participate in the annual rite of passage The theme for each group is chosen by second- and third-year students, known as “mums” and “dads”, who have been matched with the first years. The proud “parents” stand on the edge of lawn screaming and waving to their “children”. Within minutes, the smell of shaving foam fills the square as cans are emptied over other students. It quickly becomes impossible to distinguish between costumes “Traditions like this are much more important because people are less connected face to face than they were before. Getting to do something like this brings everyone together,” says Freya, a first year whose group has been dressed as periodic table elements by their chemistry student parents Simon, who is part of the same family, says: “When you are covering each other in shaving foam, how much more bonded can you get?” Everyone involved recognises that this activity is particularly strange in a crowded field of unusual university rituals. At Merton College, Oxford, students walk backwards around Fellows’ Quadrangle when the clocks go back in October. In Aberdeen, each new rector is carried around campus on the back of a stuffed bull by students There is a serious point to the St Andrews ritual at this isolated university on the east coast of Fife, the third oldest in the English-speaking world. More than half of the small town is made up of students – who come from all over the world – and the tradition helps break down barriers between students Deborah, an American medical student, is looking out at her academic children in the crowd. Her group has dressed as the blue-skinned supervillain, Megamind, from the animated DreamWorks film. “Because it’s such a small university, we get to have these sort of events. It wouldn’t be feasible at a bigger place. It brings people together. We do not have as many things going on because we are so small, so it helps create community and people you wouldn’t usually meet,” she says Sunday has always been a crucial part of the weekend tradition, when first years are woken early, “kidnapped”, and made to take a dip in the North Sea. But in 2026, that is optional. For the Monday foam fight, students are encouraged to donate to a local food bank before they start spraying from their canisters – and appears to be far less alcohol-fuelled than it has in previous years After about half an hour, the excited students running around the green begin to slow. The cans of shaving foam are empty and the first years head to the exit to be hosed down despite the single digit temperature. Away from the green, foam-covered students greet their parents with bear hugs, covering them with foam, before heading home for a shower “It’s amazing,” says Henry, an American student whose camouflage face paint has been completely covered in foam. “I only really know Americans, so getting to meet people from Singapore, England, South America, Africa and the Middle East through this is great. It’s rare to find a place where you can meet such a diverse group of people.”

selected_news.title: İstanbul Zirvesi'nde ABD-İsrail'e Saldırı Uyarısı
selected_news.summary: Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher. The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked. Continue reading...
selected_news.source_headline: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
selected_news.article_text: Multinational ‘anti-war bloc’ uses Istanbul summit to call for a diplomatic solution to Middle East crisis Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.” Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.” He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser” “We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.” Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation” “I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

selected_news.source_headline: Epstein files take back seat in midterms but experts say issue has not gone away
selected_news.article_text: Other voter concerns have prevailed but return of Congress likely to see renewed focus on late sex offender’s activities As US voters head to the polls for crucial and fraught midterm elections, some survivors’ advocates in the Jeffrey Epstein investigation have expressed concern that the scandal could recede into the background Political experts believe, however, the Epstein issue is not going away permanently and that many voters can balance day-to-day concerns such as affordability and AI with the scandal involving the late financier and accused sex trafficker whose social circle was widespread among America’s elite “My greatest concern is not that the public will forget Jeffrey Epstein, but that the politicians and institutions responsible for accountability will use the chaos of world events as an excuse to move on,” said Spencer Kuvin of Goldlaw, who has represented multiple Epstein survivors Kuvin added: “Wars, economic crises and political controversies may dominate the headlines, but they do not erase the suffering of the victims or the unanswered questions about how Epstein and his powerful associates were allowed to operate for decades “Justice should not have an expiration date, and it certainly should not be dictated by the news cycle. We cannot allow the Epstein scandal to become yesterday’s news simply because today’s headlines are more urgent.” Kuvin called for the US government to continue releasing Epstein files – which many have said were excluded from allegedly incomplete disclosures – and for Congress to demand accountability “It has been disappointing to have seen attention diverted from Jeffrey Epstein in the past year,” said Jennifer Freeman of Marsh Law, who represents numerous Epstein survivors in litigation surrounding his sexual abuse of teenage girls Freeman, however, expressed optimism about the long-term prospects of justice for survivors, saying: “While public attention may have shifted from the Epstein case, given the electoral cycle, I am confident it will command concentration and accountability shortly again.” Freeman noted that she was continuing to pursue a lawsuit against the US government for alleged negligence “in repeatedly, for decades, dropping the ball on investigating and prosecuting Epstein”. She is also litigating a class-action lawsuit against his estate related to his collection and production of child sex abuse images Political experts said that Epstein might get less attention from campaigning politicians and voters, but that it was probably a temporary dip, not a permanent drop-off “It really does feel like everything is on fire. I think people can care about several things at once, but what’s directly affecting their lives tends to take priority,” Brittany Martinez, a Republican strategist who works as acting director of Principles First, said. “When they’re worried about gas prices, living costs and whether their government is working for them, that can push Epstein out of the immediate conversation “I don’t think the questions or the demand for answers have gone away; they’re just competing for attention. So I’d expect to hear less about it for stretches, rather than see it disappear altogether.” “There’s just something every day with Trump,” said Shawn Donahue, clinical associate professor in the University at Buffalo’s department of political science For Donahue, timing also plays a key role. The US Congress has been in recess and without members on the House floor, so there’s not any discussion of the Epstein Files Transparency Act’s proposed new iteration. This bill, the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, seeks to address what advocates have said are shortfalls in the present EFTA – such as an absence of enforcement mechanisms “It kind of feels like whenever Congress comes back into session, this probably starts to become more of an issue again, and especially if Democrats are looking at being in control of one or maybe both chambers of Congress,” Donahue said Should Democrats win the house, as polls project, Donahue expects they will swiftly “put Republicans on the spot” with Epstein. “Democrats are ready to start on the investigation from day one.” For Julie Roginsky, who co-founded the non-profit Lift Our Voices and pursued a sexual harassment lawsuit against the former Fox News CEO Roger Ailes, the significance of Epstein among voters has not gone away “I think Epstein is part of the reason that Trump’s numbers are at record lows. I think it’s something that was one of the issues where even Maga Republicans broke with him,” Roginsky said. “I think that if Democrats do get control of at least one house of Congress this year, then starting next year, you’re going to see a lot more conversation about survivors and about Epstein.” Congressional supporters of survivors said they would keep fighting for truth and justice “This is bigger than a moment. It’s a reckoning, and Americans are ready to have this conversation about power, abuse, and who gets protected,” the Democratic New Mexico representative Teresa Leger Fernández said in a statement. “Of course, Americans will vote with their pocketbooks. They’re worried about groceries, gas, and making rent. But they won’t forget that this president was Epstein’s friend and tried to hide the truth from them “The survivors have fought for decades to be heard. Our responsibility is to keep fighting alongside them, get the truth out, and hold those responsible accountable. That responsibility doesn’t disappear when the headlines change.” The Massachusetts Democratic representative Ayanna Pressley said in a statement: “Justice for survivors of Epstein’s abuse has been a prominent issue amongst the electorate because people of conscience see through the cover-ups of the Trump Administration and demand accountability – that won’t change no matter how much they try to flood the zone and distract us.” Pressley and fellow representatives Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross recently introduced legislation to address survivors’ financial burdens The New Mexico Democratic senator Ben Ray Luján similarly commented that whatever might be unfolding, he would keep pushing for the files to be released in full despite the Department of Justice insisting they have released all Epstein investigative files required under the law “We cannot lose sight of the need to release the full Epstein files, hold those responsible accountable, and ensure survivors receive the justice they deserve,” Luján said Asked for comment, the White House insisted Trump had advocated for survivors “Just as President Trump has said, he’s been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee’s subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein’s Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein’s victims than anyone before him,” the White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement The statement then claimed that several Democrats had yet to explain why they were soliciting money and meetings from Epstein after he was a convicted sex offender As for the Department of Justice, the department maintains they have complied with disclosure requirements under the original EFTA. They also rejected claims by New Mexico’s attorney general, Raúl Torrez, that the justice department had not been helping the state’s investigation “The Epstein Files Transparency Act does not require, and the protective orders in place in the Southern District of New York do not permit, disclosure of victim-identifying information carte blanche, and New Mexico has provided no lawful basis to justify such sweeping disclosures,” the department said in a statement. “Protecting victim privacy remains a top priority for the Department, and neither [legal] requests nor a desire to cooperate outweighs that privacy. DOJ remains available to assist New Mexico’s investigation consistent with the law and binding court orders.”

selected_news.source_headline: Macron accused of putting France’s right to protest at risk with ‘vandal’s law’
selected_news.article_text: Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponents Emmanuel Macron has been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month of protests in which high-school students have blockaded schools demanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform Trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joining sustained street demonstrations in a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of its worst days of violence in years earlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake of violent clashes after Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was “absolutely essential” after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis. Marine Le Pen, of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring’s presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France’s highest court over her conviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds, launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to “bring back order to France” The RN has claimed the “vandals pay” bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: “Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying.” She said: “We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?” Éric Coquerel, from Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the “vandals pay” law “would mean the end of street demonstrations” in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: “No demonstration could take place again in our country.” In an open letter to Le Monde, leftwing trade unions and France’s Human Rights League wrote: “This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law.” At this weekend’s protests there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested At demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, from pension changes to same-sex marriage Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: “Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties.” He said this was “unprecedented” and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law Lecornu will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades

selected_news.title: Mary Peltola, araç kazasıyla kampanya turunu erteledi
selected_news.summary: Peltola and her family sustained minor injuries after a driver struck the car transporting group to campaign stop Mary Peltola , a Democrat who is running for Alaska ’s lone US Senate seat, and her family suffered minor injuries in a car crash while driving to a campaign stop on Saturday, her campaign said. The family was on its way to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, her campaign said in a statement on Sunday. Peltola required medical attention after the collision. Continue reading...
selected_news.source_headline: Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola delays campaign stops after car crash
selected_news.article_text: Peltola and her family sustained minor injuries after a driver struck the car transporting group to campaign stop Mary Peltola, a Democrat who is running for Alaska’s lone US Senate seat, and her family suffered minor injuries in a car crash while driving to a campaign stop on Saturday, her campaign said The family was on its way to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet when another vehicle crashed into the one transporting Peltola and her family, her campaign said in a statement on Sunday. Peltola required medical attention after the collision “Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits,” Cheryl Bruce, Peltola’s campaign manager, said in a statement. “Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover.” Bruce added: “Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families.” Police responded to a “multi-vehicle collision” at about 6.55pm on Saturday, according to the Anchorage police department. Peltola’s family and the occupant of a second vehicle were taken to a local hospital “with non-life-threatening injuries”, according to the authorities, while the occupant of a third vehicle refused medical transport “The circumstances of the collision are under investigation,” reads a statement from the police department Peltola, an Alaska Native and former congresswoman, is challenging Republican incumbent senator Dan Sullivan, hoping to become the first Democrat in nearly two decades to represent the state in the Senate. Both candidates have tried to rally support from Alaska Native voters, a key constituency in the high-stakes race that has become one of the most watched in the nation On Friday, Donald Trump ordered the justice department to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Sullivan loses. The lawsuit cites potential confusion with another Republican candidate who is listed on the ranked-choice ballot as Daniel J Sullivan Jr, who is a retired schoolteacher Peltola’s incident delayed what her campaign announced as the “Alaska Always tour,” an eight-stop push through the last week before election day. Her campaign said she will resume events on Tuesday, with a stop in Homer, Alaska

selected_news.title: Vučić, Öğrenci Hareketine Seçimi Kaybetti
selected_news.summary: The populist right-wing leader of 12 years says it is "clear" his party has lost the vote billed as a referendum on the country's future.
selected_news.source_headline: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement
selected_news.article_text: Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to the student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections "We still do not have final results... it is clear that we have lost these elections," the right-wing populist leader said as he conceded late on Sunday Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission indicated a record high turnout, which commentators had suggested would favour the student movement Vučić had called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 and was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017 He made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade There were celebrations on the streets of the city, with people dancing and chanting "victory", cars honking, and fireworks set off. "Serbia is free," one student told the BBC. "It's a miracle." The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities "This will be a free state," its lead candidate - cardiologist Ilija Srdanović - said in a statement to BBC Serbian as the result became clear He said the movement hoped to "free the country from tyranny" The anti-corruption movement campaigned on a manifesto that included purging officials who broke rules cracking down on protesters, stopping party loyalists from leading public enterprises, and freeing the public broadcaster of political control Vučić and the SNS party have repeatedly denied corruption Vučić, who backs Serbia's candidacy for the European Union while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, had pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, and investment in state healthcare Preliminary figures provided by Serbia's election commission suggested a record high turnout, with 64.9% having cast their vote by 18:00 local time (17:00 GMT), two hours before polls were set to close
